title: Programming for high change personality types
summary: Advice for people who crave novelty (he calls them 'high change' personalities, unlike his own monk-like diligence). Novices shouldn't stay on a program long, but advanced lifters can run one for years; change-seekers should pre-plan several written rotations rather than improvising in the gym, swap equipment variations, and add scenery changes like calisthenics days. Enjoyment is essential: training must never become a chore.

claims.claim: Getting better at anything physical takes consistency and repeating the same thing; over 10 years of lifting some exercises inevitably become redundant.
He has the opposite temperament: extremely diligent and happy to do the same thing a thousand times, more like a monk.
Novices shouldn't stay novices more than four to six months, so novices and early intermediates shouldn't be attached to a program.
For non-novices, staying long on one program isn't the problem; he stayed two to three years on the same program, changing internal details but not the main mechanism.
Lift rotation is becoming more popular because people have shorter attention spans, but most do it wrong.
If you need change, write several routines in advance and switch between them rather than picking random lifts on the day.
Deciding what to train on the spot makes you favour muscles you like, turning strengths into bigger strengths while weak points get weaker, and you lose track of what you hit recently.
You can keep things exciting by changing the equipment rather than the lift, e.g. thick-bar floor press or a different deadlift variation, but then you must recalibrate volume, weight and intensity.
He autoregulates his training and uses rotations, but they are well defined in his program.
Forcing a change-loving person onto a rigid program makes them miserable; spirit is as important as body in natural bodybuilding, and if it withers, gains won't hold.
A change of scenery helps: program a calisthenics day in a park on a rest or low-impact day.
He rejects the idea that training should be a grind you sometimes hate; not every day is great, but you should work to make every day pleasurable so you keep going.
The biggest trap is turning bodybuilding into a job or chore; for him that would signal the end of his journey.
